title: Constrained minimax approximation for quantum signal processing
authors: Yulong Dong, James B. Larsen, Lin Lin, Rahul Sarkar
abstract: Quantum signal processing (QSP) provides a simple and efficient framework for implementing polynomial transformations using quantum circuits. Its classical design stage leads to a constrained minimax approximation problem: find a polynomial of prescribed parity that approximates a target function uniformly on a fitting set while remaining bounded in magnitude by one on the domain $[0,1]$, which can be viewed as a semi-infinite constraint. Discretization converts the problem into a linear program, but feasibility at a set of finitely many sampled points does not ensure feasibility on the whole domain, especially when an optimal approximant reaches the boundary of the feasible set. We investigate two approaches to address this difficulty. A Remez exchange method combined with active-set constraint enforcement is efficient on many tested instances, but its stability depends on the target and problem geometry. We then introduce nonlinear Fourier retraction, which uses QSP completion and phase synthesis to turn a nearly feasible polynomial into phase factors for a feasible QSP polynomial without increasing the degree. Across representative problems, retraction largely preserves approximation accuracy and remains effective on instances where the Remez heuristic is unstable. The resulting workflow connects classical minimax approximation and semi-infinite optimization with nonlinear Fourier analysis, and is implemented in the qsppack software package.
summary: This paper tackles the mathematical challenge of constrained minimax approximation within Quantum Signal Processing (QSP). It develops and validates a nonlinear Fourier retraction technique to ensure that polynomial approximations, derived from solving large semi-infinite programs, remain physically feasible (i.e., bounded by one) while minimizing error. This provides a powerful, reliable workflow for designing practical quantum circuits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the constrained minimax approximation problem arising in Quantum Signal Processing (QSP), which requires finding a polynomial approximation that remains bounded by one on the domain while minimizing approximation error.
main_result: The authors introduce a nonlinear Fourier retraction method that successfully converts nearly feasible polynomial approximations into strictly feasible ones, maintaining high approximation accuracy even in challenging regimes.
method: The approach combines solving a Linear Semi-Infinite Program (LSIP) via discretization (LP) with a novel nonlinear Fourier retraction technique to enforce boundary constraints.
model_or_system: The context is Quantum Signal Processing (QSP), where polynomial transformations are implemented using quantum circuits. The approximation is formulated using Chebyshev polynomials ($\Phi(x)$) to construct an $	ext{SU}(2)$ valued QSP protocol.
key_observables: Approximation error ($\lVert P - g Vert_Y$), constraint violation ($\lVert \langle \hat{c}^*, \Phi angle Vert_X - 1$), and the convergence of the retraction method.
important_parameters: The degree of the polynomial ($d$), the size of the discretization sets ($|\hat{X}|, |\hat{Y}|$), and the regime of approximation (e.g., fully-coherent regime).
main_assumptions: The primary difficulty addressed is that feasibility at finite sample points does not guarantee feasibility on the entire domain, especially when the optimal approximant hits the boundary.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the comparison between the optimal (but potentially infeasible) solution and the retracted solution, showing the retraction method maintains accuracy and enforces feasibility, particularly for the threshold projector ($g_{TP}$).
paper_structure: The paper first defines the constrained minimax problem in QSP, analyzes initial discretization methods (Remez exchange), and then introduces and rigorously tests the nonlinear Fourier retraction method, demonstrating its superior performance over standard techniques.
why_interesting: The work provides a robust mathematical tool for designing quantum circuits based on function approximation, which is crucial for implementing complex quantum gates or transformations in quantum computing architectures.
